title: Don't block on async code
description: Prefer `async`/`await` all the way down; avoid blocking on async code with `.Result` or `.Wait()` — it risks thread-pool starvation and deadlocks, especially under a `SynchronizationContext`.

title: Use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code
description: Library code with no UI/request context to resume on should use `ConfigureAwait(false)` so continuations don't unnecessarily marshal back to a captured context.

title: Avoid async void outside event handlers
description: `async void` methods can't be awaited and their exceptions can't be caught by the caller — reserve the pattern for event handlers and use `async Task` everywhere else.

title: Return Task, not void, for anything awaitable
description: Any method you need to await, test, or compose with other async work should return `Task`/`Task<T>` so callers can observe completion and exceptions.

title: Reuse HttpClient instances
description: Create a single `HttpClient` (or resolve one via `IHttpClientFactory`) instead of `new HttpClient()` per call — repeated instantiation can exhaust available sockets under load.

title: Dispose deterministically with using
description: Wrap `IDisposable` resources in `using`/`await using` instead of relying on the finalizer, which runs at an unpredictable time and adds GC pressure.

title: Avoid unnecessary boxing
description: Don't box value types into non-generic collections (`ArrayList`) or through interface calls in hot paths — each box is a heap allocation and a copy.

title: Use StringBuilder for loop concatenation
description: Repeated `+=` string concatenation in a loop allocates a new string each iteration; use `StringBuilder` when building a string incrementally.

title: Prefer records for immutable data
description: Use `record` types for data-carrying types that need value equality and immutability instead of hand-rolling `Equals`/`GetHashCode` on a class.

title: Turn on nullable reference types and fix the warnings
description: Enable `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` project-wide and actually resolve the warnings it surfaces instead of suppressing them — that's where the real value is.

title: Use Span<T> for high-throughput buffer work
description: Reach for `Span<T>`/`Memory<T>` in parsing or buffer-manipulation hot paths to avoid allocating intermediate substrings or arrays.

title: Favor DI over static singletons
description: Inject dependencies rather than reaching for static singletons or service locators — it keeps code testable and dependencies explicit.

title: Keep constructors free of virtual calls
description: Calling a virtual method from a constructor can run against a derived object that isn't fully initialized yet — keep constructors non-virtual and simple.

title: Implement IEquatable<T> for hot equality checks
description: Types used as dictionary/hash-set keys or compared frequently should implement `IEquatable<T>` (or be records) to avoid the boxing/reflection cost of default `Equals`.

title: Expose read-only collection types in public APIs
description: Return `IReadOnlyList<T>`/`IReadOnlyCollection<T>` from public APIs that don't need to expose mutation, rather than a concrete `List<T>`.

title: Catch specific exceptions, not Exception
description: Avoid broad `catch (Exception)` blocks that swallow errors — catch the specific types you can actually recover from, and log/rethrow the rest.

title: Use exception filters instead of catch-and-rethrow
description: An exception filter (`catch (Ex e) when (...)`) lets you conditionally handle an exception without catching and rethrowing, which preserves the original stack trace.

title: Favor pattern matching over long if/else chains
description: Use `is`/`switch` expressions to replace long `if`/`else if` chains that check types or values — it's more concise and the compiler can flag missing cases.

title: Propagate and honor CancellationToken
description: Thread `CancellationToken` through async call chains and actually check/pass it through, rather than accepting the parameter and ignoring it.

title: Don't wrap I/O-bound work in Task.Run inside a web app
description: `Task.Run` just moves I/O-bound work to another thread-pool thread — it doesn't parallelize I/O and wastes a thread inside a request pipeline that's already async.

title: Use immutable collections for shared read-heavy state
description: Types like `ImmutableArray<T>` or `FrozenDictionary<T>` are a good fit for read-heavy, rarely-changing data accessed from multiple threads without locking.

title: Use System.Text.Json source generation for AOT/perf-sensitive code
description: `[JsonSerializable]` source-generated serializers avoid reflection at startup and are required for trimmed/Native AOT apps to serialize reliably.

title: Validate arguments at public API boundaries
description: Use `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` and similar guards at the start of public methods rather than letting bad state propagate deep into a call chain.

title: Don't use volatile as a substitute for synchronization
description: `volatile` only affects instruction reordering and visibility — it doesn't make compound operations (like increment) atomic; use proper locking for those.

title: Scope locks as tightly as possible
description: Keep the code inside a `lock`/`SemaphoreSlim` limited to the actual shared state being protected — don't hold a lock across unrelated or slow work.

title: Profile before micro-optimizing
description: Apply low-level tricks like aggressive inlining only after profiling shows a specific hot path needs it — not by default across the codebase.

title: Version public API surface deliberately
description: Treat breaking changes to a public assembly/NuGet package's API as a major-version event, and avoid silently breaking consumers between minor versions.

title: Use new syntax where it improves readability, not everywhere
description: Expression-bodied members and primary constructors read well for simple cases — don't reach for them reflexively where a normal method/constructor is clearer.

title: Keep DTOs and records free of business logic
description: Data-carrying types should carry data — business rules belong in domain/application services, not inside a record or DTO.

title: Enforce formatting and analyzers in CI
description: Run `dotnet format` and a Roslyn analyzer ruleset as a CI gate so style and common bug patterns are caught before a human reviews the PR.

title: Watch for captive dependencies
description: Never inject a scoped/transient service directly into a singleton's constructor — it gets captured for the singleton's lifetime; resolve it from a scope/factory instead.

title: Keep middleware order intentional
description: Order the pipeline deliberately: exception handling and HTTPS redirection early, authentication after routing, endpoints last — order changes behavior, not just style.

title: Never expose Kestrel directly to the internet
description: Put a reverse proxy (IIS, Nginx, YARP) in front of Kestrel for TLS termination, request buffering, and basic hardening rather than exposing it publicly on its own.

title: Use IOptionsMonitor for config that can change at runtime
description: Prefer `IOptionsMonitor<T>`/`IOptionsSnapshot<T>` over manually re-reading `IConfiguration` when settings can be reloaded without a restart.

title: Return ProblemDetails for API errors
description: Use RFC 7807 `ProblemDetails` responses for API errors instead of ad-hoc error shapes, so every client can parse errors the same way.

title: Keep controllers thin
description: A controller action should bind/validate input, call an application service, and map the result to a response — business logic belongs in the service layer.

title: Always resolve HttpClient via IHttpClientFactory
description: Inject `HttpClient` through `IHttpClientFactory` rather than instantiating it directly, to avoid DNS staleness and socket exhaustion issues.

title: Configure Data Protection for multi-instance deployments
description: Persist and share the Data Protection key ring across instances — otherwise auth cookies and antiforgery tokens silently stop validating when requests land on a different instance.

title: Point liveness and readiness probes at the right checks
description: Liveness should only fail if the process itself is broken; readiness can fail while a healthy instance is still warming up — pointing an orchestrator at the wrong one causes unnecessary restarts.

title: Honor RequestAborted in long-running actions
description: Pass `HttpContext.RequestAborted` into downstream async calls so work actually stops when a client disconnects instead of running to completion for nothing.

title: Use structured logging, not string interpolation
description: Log with `ILogger<T>` message templates (`"User {UserId} logged in"`) rather than interpolated strings, so log fields stay queryable in your log sink.

title: Cache deliberately, not by default
description: Enable response/output caching and compression on endpoints that are actually cacheable — never cache mutable or per-user data without a correct cache key.

title: Version the API from day one
description: Decide on a versioning scheme (URL segment, header, media type) before you have external clients — retrofitting it afterward is far more disruptive.

title: Scope CORS policies tightly
description: Configure CORS with the specific origins/methods/headers you need, and never combine `AllowAnyOrigin` with credentials — that combination is explicitly disallowed for good reason.

title: Use WebApplicationFactory for integration tests
description: Test through the real pipeline — routing, filters, DI — with `WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>` rather than only unit-testing controllers in isolation.

title: Drain work on graceful shutdown
description: Use `IHostApplicationLifetime`/`IHostedService.StopAsync` to finish in-flight work during shutdown instead of letting the process hard-kill active requests.

title: Put scheduled work in a hosted service
description: Background/scheduled work belongs in `IHostedService`/`BackgroundService`, not in fire-and-forget tasks kicked off from a controller action.

title: Validate at the boundary and trust it after
description: Validate input via model binding and data annotations (or FluentValidation) at the API edge, and don't re-validate ad hoc scattered through downstream layers.

title: Never block synchronously in request handling
description: Calling `.Result`, `Task.Wait()`, or blocking I/O inside a request handler starves the thread pool under concurrent load — keep the async chain unbroken.

title: Match API style to the surface's actual needs
description: Minimal APIs suit small, focused services; controller-based MVC suits larger surfaces that benefit from filters and conventions — pick per-service, not by habit.

title: Keep secrets out of appsettings.json in source control
description: Use user-secrets locally and a vault or managed identity in production rather than committing connection strings or API keys to `appsettings.json`.

title: Set explicit request limits and timeouts
description: Don't rely on framework defaults for request body size and timeouts on public-facing endpoints, especially ones accepting file uploads.

title: Prefer constructor injection over [FromServices] for core dependencies
description: Constructor injection keeps a controller's dependencies visible in one place; reserve `[FromServices]` for occasional per-action needs.

title: Propagate correlation IDs across service calls
description: Instrument with distributed tracing and correlation IDs so a single request can be followed end-to-end across services, not just within one service's logs.

title: Use content negotiation instead of parallel endpoints per format
description: Let the `Accept` header drive response format via content negotiation rather than building separate endpoints for JSON, XML, etc.

title: Apply rate limiting before you need it
description: Add rate-limiting middleware to public or expensive endpoints proactively, rather than reacting to the first abuse incident.

title: Verify trimmed/AOT output, don't just trust the build
description: Reflection-based libraries can silently break under trimming or Native AOT — actually run the published output's test suite, not just the untrimmed build.

title: Scope DbContext per request
description: Keep EF Core's `DbContext` scoped to a single request/unit of work — never share one instance across concurrent requests.

title: Add global exception-handling middleware
description: Use exception-handling middleware (or `IExceptionHandler`) so any unhandled exception returns a consistent, non-leaking error response instead of a raw stack trace.

title: Load-test your health checks too
description: A health check that queries the database can itself become a bottleneck under load — include health/readiness endpoints in load testing, not just business endpoints.

title: Apply Single Responsibility at the function level
description: A function should do one thing you can describe without using the word "and" — if you need "and", it's probably doing too much.

title: Prefer guard clauses over deep nesting
description: Return early on invalid/edge cases at the top of a function instead of wrapping the main logic in nested conditionals.

title: Name things for what they represent
description: Choose names that describe intent (`GetActiveUsers()`) rather than implementation detail (`GetUsersWhereFlag1True()`).

title: Keep functions short enough to review at a glance
description: If reviewing a function requires scrolling, it's a signal the function is doing more than one job and should be split.

title: Comment the why, not the what
description: Well-named code already shows what it does; a comment earns its place by explaining a non-obvious constraint, workaround, or business rule.

title: Write tests alongside the code, not after
description: Writing tests as you build a feature (or before, in TDD) catches design problems early instead of after the implementation has hardened around them.

title: Favor composition when you just need reuse
description: Reach for composition, not inheritance, when the goal is code reuse rather than modeling a genuine is-a relationship.

title: Optimize only what profiling shows is slow
description: Measure before optimizing — intuition about what's slow is frequently wrong, and premature optimization adds complexity for no measured benefit.

title: Wait for a third case before abstracting
description: Introduce a shared abstraction once you have at least two or three concrete cases that need it (rule of three) — not on the first hint of similarity.

title: Automate style instead of debating it in review
description: Let a linter/formatter enforce consistent style so reviewers spend their attention on correctness and design, not spacing and casing.

title: Fail fast on bad input
description: Validate inputs and preconditions at the start of a function so invalid state is caught immediately instead of propagating and surfacing somewhere confusing later.

title: Name magic values
description: Replace unexplained literals (`if (status == 3)`) with named constants or enums that describe what the value means.

title: Keep side effects explicit and localized
description: A method named `GetX` shouldn't also mutate shared state or write to a database — separate queries from commands.

title: Delete dead code instead of commenting it out
description: Version control already preserves history — commented-out code just adds noise and eventually goes stale and misleading.

title: Document what the code genuinely can't show
description: Reserve a README or doc comment for things a reader can't infer from the code itself (deployment steps, non-obvious tradeoffs) — don't restate the obvious.

title: Handle errors where there's enough context to act
description: Don't catch an exception just to make a method appear not to throw — handle it where the code actually knows what recovery looks like.

title: Name tests after behavior, not implementation
description: A test named "returns 404 when the id doesn't exist" survives a refactor that a test named "Test_Method1" doesn't.

title: Avoid clever one-liners over clear code
description: Nested ternaries and dense one-liners save a few lines but cost readers time every time they're read — prefer the clearer version.

title: Treat warnings as errors in CI
description: An ignored compiler or linter warning is effectively a bug report nobody reads — fail the build on new warnings instead.

title: Keep environment-specific values out of code
description: Configuration that differs by environment belongs in config/environment variables, not hardcoded constants recompiled per environment.

title: Design operations to be idempotent where practical
description: Anything that might be retried — a message handler, a migration, a webhook receiver — should be safe to run more than once with the same effect.

title: Make dependencies explicit via injection
description: Pass dependencies in rather than reaching for hidden global/static state — it makes the code's requirements visible and testable.

title: Keep pull requests small and focused
description: A PR scoped to one logical change is easier to review thoroughly and easier to revert cleanly if it causes a problem.

title: Record the why behind unusual decisions
description: Capture the reasoning for a non-obvious technical choice in an ADR or commit message — otherwise it gets re-litigated or reverted by someone who didn't know why it was done that way.

title: Don't force a shared abstraction onto coincidental similarity
description: DRY applies to actual duplicated business rules, not code that merely looks alike today but represents different concerns that will diverge.

title: Prefer strongly-typed models over dynamic/dictionaries
description: Passing `dynamic` or loosely-typed dictionaries between layers defers type errors to runtime — a proper model catches them at compile time.

title: Reserve Error-level logs for things that need attention
description: Log expected/handled conditions at Info or Warning — flooding Error-level logs with routine events trains people to ignore alerts.

title: Write for the reader debugging an incident at 2am
description: Optimize code clarity for the stressed reader under time pressure, not for the person who already understands it because they wrote it.

title: Automate what discipline alone won't sustain
description: Formatting, dependency updates, and changelog entries should be automated — relying on every developer to remember them consistently doesn't scale.

title: Refactor incrementally as you touch code
description: Apply the boy scout rule — leave code a little better each time you're in it — instead of waiting for a big-bang rewrite that rarely gets scheduled.

title: Let tooling catch style, humans catch design
description: Automate formatting and linting so reviewers spend their limited attention on correctness, design, and edge cases instead of spacing and casing.

title: Keep pull requests small
description: Review quality drops sharply on large diffs — aim for PRs under a few hundred changed lines where the change is separable.

title: Explain why in the PR description
description: The diff already shows what changed — the description should carry the reasoning, the alternatives considered, and any tradeoffs made.

title: Actually run non-trivial changes, don't just read the diff
description: For anything beyond a trivial change, check the branch out and exercise it — some bugs are invisible in a diff view.

title: Separate blocking feedback from nitpicks
description: Prefix optional suggestions (e.g. "nit:") so the author can tell at a glance what must be addressed before merge versus what's a take-it-or-leave-it idea.

title: Review test coverage, not just production code
description: Untested logic is a gap in the review itself — check that new behavior has tests, not only that the implementation looks right.

title: Explain your reasoning when responding to feedback
description: Reply with why you made a change (or didn't) rather than just pushing a fix silently — it lets the reviewer verify intent, not just the diff.

title: Don't rubber-stamp what you didn't read
description: An approval is a statement you'd stand behind the change — approving without understanding it defeats the purpose of review.

title: Set a review turnaround expectation
description: A same-business-day SLA for first review keeps PRs from stalling and authors from context-switching away and losing momentum.

title: Review for security, not just function
description: Check input validation, authorization checks, and secret handling explicitly during review — these are easy to miss when scanning only for correctness.

title: Ask before asserting when unsure
description: If an approach looks wrong but you might be missing context, ask a question first rather than stating it's incorrect outright.

title: Use draft PRs for early direction feedback
description: Open a draft PR to get feedback on approach before investing in a fully polished implementation that might need to change direction.

title: Flag technical debt even in working code
description: Call out a missing index, an N+1 query, or an unbounded cache even if the PR functions correctly today — it will cost more to fix later.

title: Make comments actionable
description: "This could be clearer" is less useful than a concrete suggested rewording the author can accept or push back on directly.

title: Move design debates out of the comment thread
description: When a review comment turns into a design discussion, take it to a call and summarize the resolution back in the PR for the record.

title: Require a reviewer with context on the affected area
description: Route reviews to someone who understands the area being changed, not just whoever is fastest to approve.

title: Scrutinize test assertions as carefully as the implementation
description: A test that can never fail provides false confidence and is arguably worse than having no test at all.

title: Gate human review behind CI status
description: Let build, test, and static analysis results pass before spending reviewer time — don't have humans catch what automation already would.

title: Propose an alternative when you disagree
description: Pair disagreement with a concrete alternative and its tradeoff, rather than only flagging that something is wrong.

title: Re-review promptly after changes land
description: A PR that addressed feedback deserves the same turnaround as the original review — don't let follow-ups sit longer than the first pass.

title: Check consistency with existing codebase patterns
description: New code that works in isolation but diverges from established conventions creates long-term maintenance cost — flag it during review.

title: Call out good decisions, not only problems
description: Positive feedback in review reinforces the practices you want repeated, not just corrects the ones you don't.

title: Don't review while rushed or fatigued
description: A distracted 5-minute review catches less than a focused 15-minute one done later — schedule review time deliberately.

title: Check edge cases, not just the happy path
description: Confirm empty input, null, timeout, and partial-failure scenarios are handled — these are the cases most often missing from a first draft.

title: Flag missing documentation on public APIs
description: Undocumented public interfaces are cheaper to fix during review than after other teams start depending on the undocumented behavior.

title: Keep a shared checklist for recurring review concerns
description: A written checklist (security, migrations, breaking changes) means review quality doesn't depend entirely on one reviewer's memory.

title: Treat review feedback as data about the codebase, not criticism
description: Recurring feedback usually points to a codebase or process gap worth fixing at the source, not just a personal correction.

title: Don't approve past unresolved must-fix comments
description: If a blocking comment truly can't be addressed before merge, track it as an explicit fast-follow ticket rather than silently approving over it.

title: Rotate reviewers across the team
description: Spreading review responsibility avoids both a single-person bottleneck and knowledge concentrating in just one reviewer.

title: Require domain sign-off for high-risk changes
description: Changes touching auth, payments, or migrations deserve a second reviewer or a specific owner's sign-off beyond the standard review.

title: Choose a branching model deliberately
description: Pick trunk-based development, GitHub flow, or Git flow based on your actual release cadence, and document the choice — don't let it emerge by accident.

title: Keep feature branches short-lived
description: Branches open for days, not weeks, minimize merge conflicts and drift from `main`, and keep code review scoped to a reviewable size.

title: Sync from main frequently, not once at the end
description: Merge or rebase `main` into your feature branch regularly so conflicts surface early and in small pieces, not all at once before the PR.

title: Use feature flags instead of long-lived branches
description: Merge incomplete work behind a feature flag so `main` stays current and the branch stays short-lived, rather than isolating work for weeks.

title: Protect main with required checks and reviews
description: No direct pushes to `main`/release branches — require passing CI and at least one review before merge.

title: Name branches for intent
description: A branch name like `fix/checkout-timeout-bug` tells a teammate what it's for; `jsmith-patch-1` tells them nothing.

title: Match merge strategy to branch lifespan
description: Squash-merge short, tidy feature branches for a clean history; use merge commits for long-running branches where the individual commit history matters.

title: Never force-push a shared branch without coordinating
description: Rewriting history that others have already pulled causes silent divergence and lost work unless everyone knows to re-sync.

title: Cut release branches only when you need to stabilize
description: Reserve release branches for when `main` needs to keep moving while a release is being stabilized — don't default to one for every change.

title: Keep commit messages clear regardless of convention
description: Whether or not you adopt Conventional Commits for tooling, every commit message should explain what changed and why in a way a future reader can act on.

title: Tag releases explicitly
description: Tag the exact commit that shipped (`v1.4.0`) rather than relying on branch names or memory to reconstruct what's in production.

title: Delete merged branches promptly
description: A branch list cluttered with long-merged branches makes it harder to see what's actually still in flight.

title: Hotfix from the deployed tag, not from a moved-on main
description: If `main` has advanced past what's in production, branch the hotfix from the release tag so you don't accidentally ship unrelated in-flight changes.

title: Route even tiny fixes through the same PR process
description: Direct commits to `main`, even for "trivial" changes, skip the review and CI gate that exists precisely to catch small mistakes.

title: Rebase before merging when it's safe
description: Rebasing a feature branch onto `main` before merge keeps history linear and readable, as long as the branch isn't shared with others mid-rebase.

title: Keep branches about code, not environment
description: Environment-specific configuration belongs in config/environment variables, not in separate long-lived branches per environment.

title: Keep commits at one logical change each
description: Consistent commit granularity keeps `git bisect` and selective reverts useful — a commit mixing three unrelated changes defeats both.

title: Avoid long-lived integration branches
description: A branch that diverges from `main` for weeks before merging recreates the same merge pain trunk-based development is meant to avoid.

title: Run CI on the branch, not just after merge
description: Catch breakage before it lands in `main` by requiring the branch's own CI run to pass, not relying on post-merge detection.

title: Document conflict resolution for generated files
description: Lock files and generated migrations conflict often and naive resolution can silently corrupt them — write down the correct resolution procedure.

title: Open draft PRs early for visibility
description: A draft PR against a feature branch shares progress and invites early comment without requesting a full review yet.

title: Keep main always deployable
description: Trunk-based development's actual point is that `main` can be deployed at any time — treat any state that breaks that as an incident, not a style preference.

title: Prefer revert over force-push for a bad deployed commit
description: Reverting a merged, deployed commit is safer and more auditable than force-pushing `main` to erase it.

title: Balance branch protection against review latency
description: Required checks and reviews should catch real risk — too many gates on every branch makes even trivial fixes take hours to land.

title: Scope CI to affected paths in a monorepo
description: Run only the checks relevant to what actually changed in a monorepo branch, so feedback time doesn't grow with the size of the whole repo.

title: Keep migrations coupled to the code that needs them
description: Ship a migration in the same branch/PR as the code depending on it, and make it backward-compatible to support a zero-downtime rolling deploy.

title: Don't merge past known-failing tests to unblock a deploy
description: Merging with red CI "just this once" erodes everyone's trust that a green `main` actually means something.

title: Encode the ticket ID in branch names
description: A convention like `feat/JIRA-123-add-export` makes any branch traceable back to the work item that justified it.

title: Audit stale branches periodically
description: Branches with no commits in months should be revived, merged, or deleted — not left indefinitely as clutter and confusion.

title: Scale branch protection to repository risk
description: A shared library used by many teams warrants stricter required checks than an internal tool only one team touches.

title: Avoid SELECT * in application code
description: Select only the columns you actually need — it reduces I/O, avoids breaking on schema changes, and lets covering indexes actually cover the query.

title: Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY
description: Add indexes for the columns that actually drive filtering, joining, and sorting on large tables, and confirm the benefit with an execution plan rather than assuming.

title: Keep indexed columns sargable in WHERE clauses
description: Wrapping an indexed column in a function (`WHERE YEAR(CreatedAt) = 2024`) prevents an index seek — rewrite as a range comparison the optimizer can use.

title: Always parameterize queries
description: String-concatenated SQL is both a SQL-injection vector and defeats the database's query plan cache — use parameters every time, no exceptions.

title: Prefer set-based operations over row-by-row loops
description: A cursor or application-side loop processing one row at a time scales far worse than an equivalent set-based `UPDATE`/`INSERT` statement.

title: Keep transactions as short as possible
description: A long-running transaction holds its locks the whole time — minimize the work inside it to reduce blocking of other queries.

title: Use EXISTS instead of COUNT(*) > 0
description: `EXISTS` can stop scanning at the first match; `COUNT(*) > 0` typically has to count all matches first for no benefit when you only need a yes/no.

title: Avoid implicit type conversions in comparisons
description: Comparing a column to a literal of a different type (`WHERE VarcharCol = 123`) can silently disable index usage on that column.

title: Use covering indexes for critical queries
description: A covering index lets the engine satisfy a frequently-run query entirely from the index, without a lookup back to the base table.

title: Batch large bulk updates and deletes
description: Running one massive `UPDATE`/`DELETE` against millions of rows can blow out the transaction log and lock contention — batch it into smaller chunks.

title: Keep statistics current
description: Stale statistics make the query optimizer misjudge row counts and pick bad plans as the underlying data grows — ensure auto-update is on or refresh manually after bulk loads.

title: Use NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN with a nullable subquery
description: `NOT IN` against a subquery that can return `NULL` silently returns zero rows for the whole query — `NOT EXISTS` doesn't have this trap.

title: Paginate at the query level
description: Use `OFFSET`/`FETCH` or keyset pagination in the query itself rather than loading a full result set and paging it in application code.

title: Be explicit about join types
description: An accidental cross join or the wrong join type is one of the most common sources of duplicated or missing rows in a result set.

title: Watch for N+1 queries from an ORM
description: A loop that triggers one query per iteration should be replaced with eager loading, an explicit join, or a projection that fetches everything in one round trip.

title: Enforce integrity with constraints, not just app code
description: Foreign keys and `CHECK` constraints catch bad data regardless of which application or script wrote it — don't rely on application code alone.

title: Rewrite correlated subqueries as joins where possible
description: A correlated subquery in the `SELECT` list re-executes per outer row on large result sets — an equivalent `JOIN` is usually far cheaper.

title: Review indexes for unused or duplicate ones periodically
description: Every index adds write cost — an index that's never used by any query plan is pure overhead and should be dropped.

title: Prefer UNION ALL unless you need de-duplication
description: Plain `UNION` forces an extra sort/distinct pass to remove duplicates — use `UNION ALL` when you know the sets don't overlap or duplicates are fine.

title: Test query changes against realistic data volume
description: A plan that looks fine against a small dev database can degrade badly at production scale — test against a representative row count before shipping.

title: Avoid leading-wildcard LIKE searches on large tables
description: `LIKE '%term'` can't use a standard b-tree index efficiently — consider full-text search or a trigram index for that access pattern instead.

title: Isolate analytical queries from transactional load
description: Route heavy reporting queries to a read replica or dedicated reporting store so they don't degrade OLTP performance for the primary workload.

title: Verify execution plans before and after a change
description: Check the actual execution plan when adding an index or rewriting a query, not just whether the query returns the right rows.

title: Make migrations additive first, cleanup later
description: Add new columns/tables in a backward-compatible way and defer destructive cleanup to a later migration, so old and new app versions can run side by side during a rolling deploy.

title: Fix the join, don't paper over duplicates with DISTINCT
description: `SELECT DISTINCT` used to hide duplicate rows from a bad join usually means the join's cardinality is wrong — fix that instead of masking the symptom.

title: Choose appropriately sized data types
description: Storing dates as strings or defaulting every text column to `NVARCHAR(MAX)` costs both storage and index efficiency — pick types that match the actual data.

title: Use window functions for running totals and ranking
description: `ROW_NUMBER()`, `SUM() OVER(...)`, and similar window functions usually outperform and outread an equivalent self-join or correlated subquery.

title: Monitor slow queries proactively
description: Review query store or slow-query logs on a schedule instead of only investigating performance after someone complains.

title: Avoid stacking views many levels deep
description: Deeply nested views make it hard for the optimizer to produce a good plan and hard for a human to debug what's actually being queried.

title: Grant applications least-privilege database access
description: An application connecting as `sa`/`db_owner` by default has far more access than it needs — scope its credentials to the specific tables/operations it performs.

title: Apply least privilege by default
description: Grant only the permissions a user or service actually needs, and expand from there deliberately — never start broad and plan to narrow later.

title: Assign permissions through roles, not per-user hacks
description: Use RBAC or ABAC so access can be reviewed and reasoned about, instead of scattering individual per-user permission checks through the codebase.

title: Never commit secrets to source control
description: API keys, connection strings, and certificates belong in a secrets manager or vault with access auditing, never in a repository — even a private one.

title: Prefer managed identity over static credentials
description: Use managed/workload identities for service-to-service auth in the cloud instead of long-lived static keys that have to be stored and rotated manually.

title: Require MFA for privileged accounts at minimum
description: Every administrative or highly privileged account should require MFA, with a roadmap toward requiring it for all users.

title: Rotate credentials on a schedule and on suspicion
description: Set a defined rotation cadence for keys and credentials, and rotate immediately on suspected compromise or when someone with access leaves.

title: Prefer short-lived tokens over static ones
description: Use OAuth access tokens, SAS tokens, or similar short-lived credentials wherever the protocol supports them instead of a permanent static secret.

title: Validate all external input at the trust boundary
description: Never trust client-supplied data — including hidden form fields and headers — validate and sanitize it where it enters the system.

title: Log authorization decisions for audit
description: Record who accessed what and whether it was allowed, not just application errors — it's what makes incident response and compliance audits possible.

title: Separate duties for sensitive operations
description: The person who can approve a production deploy shouldn't also be the only one who can alter the audit trail of that deploy.

title: Use just-in-time access instead of standing admin rights
description: Grant elevated access only for the duration it's needed rather than leaving privileged roles active and unused most of the time.

title: Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit by default
description: Treat encryption as the baseline for all sensitive data, not an opt-in reserved for projects someone flagged as "sensitive".

title: Default to deny in access and network policies
description: Explicitly allow what's needed rather than trying to enumerate and block everything that's known-bad — default-allow policies age poorly.

title: Scope IAM policies to specific resources
description: Avoid wildcard resource grants (`*`) even for development convenience — scope policies to the specific resource IDs/ARNs a role actually needs.

title: Review access on a regular cadence
description: Audit unused accounts, stale service principals, and orphaned permissions periodically, not only when a compliance audit forces the question.

title: Manage access at the group/role level
description: Assigning permissions to groups instead of individuals keeps access reviewable and consistent as people move between teams.

title: Add conditional access for sensitive systems
description: Require signals like device compliance or sign-in risk in addition to a password for access to sensitive systems, not a password check alone.

title: Centralize identity through an IdP
description: Use SSO via an identity provider (Entra ID, Okta) instead of maintaining separate local credential stores per application.

title: Enforce authorization at every reachable layer
description: Apply the same auth checks at the API, admin panel, and background job trigger level — don't rely on the UI being the only gate to a sensitive action.

title: Classify data and match controls to sensitivity
description: Apply stronger controls to more sensitive data rather than treating all data uniformly — classification should drive the control, not the other way around.

title: Design every grant to be quickly revocable
description: A token, role assignment, or shared credential should be revocable on its own, without requiring a system-wide credential rotation to shut off access.

title: Treat anything shipped to a client as public
description: Never embed secrets in client-side code, mobile apps, or CI logs — anything that reaches a client or a log should be assumed to be exposed.

title: Use one service account per application
description: A dedicated service principal per application scopes blast radius and keeps auditing meaningful, versus one shared account used by several systems.

title: Rate-limit and lock out authentication attempts
description: Backoff and lockout on repeated failed logins slow down credential-stuffing and brute-force attacks against your authentication endpoints.

title: Patch known vulnerabilities on a schedule
description: Most real-world breaches exploit known, unpatched CVEs rather than novel zero-days — keep dependencies and base images current on a defined cadence.

title: Review IAM policy changes like code
description: Permission grants are high-impact — require peer review and change management for IAM policy edits themselves, not just application code.

title: Isolate environments with separate credentials
description: Dev, test, and prod should use separate access boundaries so a compromised dev credential can't reach production.

title: Prefer delegated OAuth scopes over sharing one powerful credential
description: Federated, scoped authorization limits what a compromised integration can do, versus one broad credential shared across multiple integrations.

title: Plan incident response assuming leaks happen
description: Have a tested process to revoke and rotate credentials quickly — prevention matters, but assume it will eventually fail and plan the response too.

title: Test your break-glass procedure
description: Document and periodically test the emergency access path that must work even when your normal IdP/SSO is unavailable.
